answer: Interviews is the most commonly used technique for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects.

payload.hypothesis: Interviews is the most commonly used technique for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects: 50.000% of the 194 valid Q9 respondents (97/194; 35.145% of all 276) reported using interviews, the highest of any elicitation technique, with a nonparametric percentile bootstrap 95% CI of [42.784%, 57.216%]. The 69.399% / [69.062, 69.735] figure stated in the question cannot be reproduced from this file as a single-technique respondent proportion at any reasonable denominator, and its CI width implies a different resampling unit or dataset version.
payload.workflow: Loaded the 276-row survey CSV. Identified the six Q9_ML_Elicitation_* flag columns; each uses a binary presence flag {quoted, not quoted} plus a '-77' no-response sentinel. Excluded the 82 '-77' no-response respondents (identical across all six columns) to obtain 194 valid Q9 respondents as the primary base (all-276 as sensitivity). Defined 'used' := value == 'quoted' (no Likert scale exists in the file, so no top-box threshold applies). Computed per-technique quoted counts and percentages over both bases: Interviews 97 (50.000%/35.145%), Scenarios 75 (38.660%/27.174%), Prototyping 75 (38.660%/27.174%), Workshops/Meetings 74 (38.144%/26.812%), Observation 64 (32.990%/23.188%), Others 11 (5.670%/3.986%). Identified Interviews as the most-used technique under every denominator. Ran a nonparametric percentile bootstrap (B=10000, seed=2024) resampling the 194 valid respondents to obtain 95% CIs per technique; Interviews = 50.000% [42.784%, 57.216%]. Verified the question's 69.399% is not reproducible as a single-technique proportion (max 50.000% at the valid base) and that its CI half-width (0.3365 pp) would require an effective n ~72,049 vs N=194, so that figure/CI implies a different resampling unit or dataset version. Nearest data statistic to 69.399% is the composite 'used >=2 techniques' = 135/194 = 69.588% (not a single technique).
